Doenjang-Garlic Moksal Gui

Moksal — pork collar, the shoulder's marble — is the connoisseur's cut of the tabletop: tender-firm with a fine fat weave that stands up to the grill better than loin ever will.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant. Moksal — pork collar, the shoulder's marble — is the connoisseur's cut of the tabletop: tender-firm with a fine fat weave that stands up to the grill better than loin ever will. Its natural partner is doenjang, the fermented soybean paste most Western kitchens only meet in jjigae. As a marinade base, doenjang gives pork what gochujang cannot: deep savory funk with almost no sugar, nothing to burn, and a crust that browns like a steak's instead of lacquering. This is the quiet record of the pork list — the one the regulars order.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Work the doenjang loose first. It is a stiff paste; whisk it with the soy, sesame oil, and mirin until smooth before the garlic and ginger join, or you will chase lumps through the marinade forever.
  • Marinate 2–4 hours, refrigerated. Moksal is forgiving, but past four hours the paste's salt begins curing the surface — pull back to two if your doenjang runs salty.
  • While the grill heats: set out the cold banchan. Rich cut, hot fire, cold crunch — the table plan in six words.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-high. The slices go on in a single layer; with almost no sugar in the marinade, the grill boss is building crust, not managing lacquer. First side undisturbed 2–3 minutes. Checkpoint — the smell is roasted soybean and garlic over browning pork — deeper and darker than any other record at this grill. The underside should be crusty brown and release cleanly.
  2. 02
    Flip once, 2 minutes more, pull when the meat's juices bead at the surface and the slice is just firm to a fingertip press. Rest the batch 1 minute; moksal carries a little and finishes gently. Checkpoint — test piece: crusty edge, juicy interior with a firm-but-tender chew that loin never gives, and the doenjang's savory depth arriving right behind the pork. No sweetness ahead of the meat — if there is, the honey ran heavy.
  3. 03
    Scissors into bite pieces, warm platter, straight into ssam with ssamjang or wrapped plain with rice and a strand of musaengchae in the bite. Checkpoint — the ssam test: the crust and the chew are the record's signature — this should taste like the grown-up table at the restaurant, the one that skipped the sweet marinades on purpose. Chef’s Note — if your only acquaintance with doenjang is stew, meeting it as a marinade is a small conversion experience: on dry heat, its fermented edge deepens instead of dissolving, and it browns into a crust that tastes somewhere between steak seasoning and miso butter. Buy the tub from a Korean market with a turnover — doenjang is a living paste and the fresh one is noticeably rounder than the decade-old jar at the back of an international aisle.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Marinade lumpyDoenjang not loosened firstWhisk paste with liquids before aromatics
Too saltySalty doenjang plus soyDrop the soy to 2 tsp; 2-hour marinate
Tough slicesCut with the grain or overcookedAgainst the grain, 7 mm; pull at bead-and-press
Bland crustMarinate too shortFull 2 hours minimum; grate the garlic fine

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated slices keep 24 hours. Cooked, 3 days — cold moksal over rice with a fried egg is the intended leftover, the crust softening into the yolk.
  • Variations: a teaspoon of gochujang stirred into the marinade warms it toward #M11's lane; the same marinade on chicken thighs (#M17's register); leftover marinade simmered 3 minutes into a spoon-sauce for the platter.
